content: The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) has published recommendations for the prevention and control of seasonal influenza for the 2023-2024 influenza season. Receiving an annual flu vaccine is the most effective way to protect yourself and your loved ones from influenza. This is particularly critical for individuals at higher risk of developing severe flu-related complications. Vaccination not only reduces the likelihood of contracting the flu but also decreases the risk of hospitalization or death due to influenza. Adults Aged 65 Years and Older Individuals aged 65 years and older are at a significantly higher risk of experiencing severe complications from influenza compared to younger, healthier adults. This population should prioritize receiving the flu vaccine to mitigate these risks. Adults with Chronic Health Conditions Adults with certain chronic medical conditions are also at increased risk for severe flu complications. These conditions include: Asthma: Chronic inflammation of the airways can exacerbate flu symptoms and lead to severe respiratory complications. Heart Disease and Stroke: Cardiovascular conditions increase the risk of flu-related complications, including heart attacks and strokes. Diabetes: Both type 1 and type 2 diabetes can impair the immune response, making it harder to fight off infections like the flu. Chronic Kidney Disease: Impaired kidney function can weaken the immune system, increasing susceptibility to severe flu outcomes. Pregnancy Pregnant individuals are more vulnerable to serious flu complications due to physiological changes in the immune system, heart, and lungs during pregnancy. Influenza can also pose risks to the developing fetus, making vaccination during pregnancy essential. Young Children Children under the age of 5, particularly those younger than 2 years old, are at a higher risk of severe flu complications. Infants under 6 months of age have the highest rates of hospitalization and mortality due to influenza. Other High-Risk Groups The following groups are also at increased risk for severe flu complications: Individuals with neurologic and neurodevelopmental conditions, such as epilepsy or cerebral palsy. People with blood disorders, including sickle cell disease. Those with chronic lung diseases, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or cystic fibrosis. Individuals with endocrine disorders, such as diabetes mellitus. People with liver disorders or metabolic disorders, including inherited metabolic conditions and mitochondrial disorders. Individuals with a body mass index (BMI) of 40 kg/m² or higher. People under 19 years of age who are on long-term aspirin or salicylate-containing medications, as they are at risk for Reye’s syndrome if they contract the flu. Individuals with a weakened immune system due to diseases like HIV/AIDS or cancer, or due to medications such as chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or chronic corticosteroids. People who have experienced a stroke. Additional High-Risk Populations Pregnant individuals and those up to two weeks postpartum. Residents of nursing homes and long-term care facilities. Individuals from certain racial and ethnic minority groups, including non-Hispanic Black persons, Hispanic or Latino persons, and American Indian or Alaska Native persons, who are at higher risk of flu-related hospitalization. Resources for Specific Groups The CDC provides tailored information and resources for various groups, including: Parents of young children, offering advice on keeping children healthy during flu season. Health care workers, emphasizing the importance of flu vaccination for those in medical professions. Public health and health care professionals, with guidance on vaccination, infection control, prevention, treatment, and diagnosis of influenza. Schools and childcare providers, with materials to prevent flu outbreaks and address common questions. Businesses and employers, offering workplace-specific flu prevention guidelines and printable resources. Legal professionals and policymakers, with legal materials related to influenza prevention and control. Flu Vaccine Finder The CDC encourages everyone aged 6 months and older to receive a flu vaccine. A Flu Vaccine Finder tool is available to help locate vaccination sites in your area.
